extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/early-graduate mathematics students learning probability (martingales) and multivariable calculus/differential forms
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, theorems, and example constructions for martingales, stopping times, Doob convergence and optional stopping; plus introductory material on total derivatives, partials, higher derivatives and differential forms. Useful for solving probability problems via martingale methods and for learning calculus on manifolds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Martingale property (conditional expectation criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence (Xt) is a martingale if for each t the conditional expectation E(Xt | X0, ..., Xt−1) equals Xt−1 (i.e., the expected increment given the past is zero).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (a) Simple symmetric random walk Xt (position after t fair ±1 steps) is a martingale since E(Xt | past) = Xt−1. (b) A gambler's strategy where every bet has expected value 0 yields a martingale. Use this criterion to check constructions and to modify sequences so the conditional expectation equals the previous value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supermartingale and submartingale inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence (Xt) is a supermartingale if E(Xt | past) ≤ Xt−1; a submartingale if E(Xt | past) ≥ Xt−1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Repeated games with negative expected value (house edge), e.g. repeated blackjack, produce a supermartingale for wealth Xt. The sign determines inequalities in Optional Stopping conclusions (E[Xτ] ≤ E[X0] for supermartingales, ≥ for submartingales).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicative martingale construction (product of independent mean-1 variables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X1, X2, ... be independent integrable random variables with mean 1. Then Yn := X1 X2 ··· Xn is a martingale because E(Yn | Y1, ..., Yn−1) = Yn−1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use independence and unit mean to show E(Xn | past)=1, so multiplying maintains the martingale property; practical tool for building multiplicative martingales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounded martingale converges a.s. (heuristic statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a martingale is bounded, then it will almost surely converge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as an intuition before the formal Doob convergence theorem; boundedness of the process implies the sup of expected absolute values is finite, so Doob's theorem applies. Use boundedness as a quick sufficient condition for almost sure convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doob's martingale convergence theorem (42.4.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X0, X1, ... be a supermartingale on a probability space with sup_{n≥0} E[|Xn|] < ∞. Then there exists X∞ with Xn → X∞ almost surely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesis: uniform integrability in the form of a finite uniform bound on E|Xn|. Conclusion: almost-sure convergence of the sequence. This is a central convergence criterion used when proving limits of stopped processes or infinite-time behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stopping time definition (42.5.1) and stopped process
rubrics_metrics.description: A stopping time τ : Ω → {0,1,2,...} ∪ {∞} relative to a filtration F0 ⊆ F1 ⊆ ... satisfies that for each integer n the set {ω | τ(ω) = n} is Fn-measurable. For each n ≥ 0 define X_{τ ∧ n}(ω) = X_{min{τ(ω),n}}(ω). The eventual value X_τ is defined to be X_{τ(ω)} if τ(ω) ≠ ∞, lim_{n→∞} Xn(ω) if τ(ω)=∞ and the limit exists, and otherwise undefined; the undefined case is only allowed on a null set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key measurability requirement: the decision to stop at time n must be based only on information up to time n. The stopped process X_{τ∧n} freezes the process after stopping. Ensure almost-everywhere well-definedness of X_τ (use convergence theorems or show undefined cases have measure zero).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stopped supermartingale remains a supermartingale (Proposition 42.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X0, X1, ... is a supermartingale and τ is a stopping time, then the stopped sequence X_{τ ∧ 0}, X_{τ ∧ 1}, ... is itself a supermartingale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: conditional expectations split according to whether τ equals the current index; use the supermartingale inequality on the active part to obtain E(X_{τ∧n} | F_{n−1}) ≤ X_{τ∧n−1}. This is the technical tool that justifies applying optional stopping to stopped processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doob's Optional Stopping Theorem (42.5.3) — hypotheses and conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X0, X1, ... be a supermartingale with filtration F0 ⊆ F1 ⊆ ... and τ a stopping time. If any one of the following holds for some constant C: (a) Finite time: τ(ω) ≤ C a.s.; (b) Finite money: for each n ≥ 1, |X_{τ∧n}(ω)| ≤ C a.s.; (c) Finite bets: E[τ] < ∞ and for each n≥1 the conditional expectation E(|Xn − X_{n−1}| | Fn) takes values at most C a.s. on {τ ≥ n}. Then X_τ is well-defined a.e. and E[X_τ] ≤ E[X0].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each hypothesis gives a sufficient control to pass expectations through stopping; choose the hypothesis appropriate to your application (bounded stopping time, uniform boundedness of stopped values, or control on expected increments plus finite expected stopping time). For submartingale/martingale variants, reverse/equality conclusions follow (see corollary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheeky interpretation: 'the only winning move is not to play'
rubrics_metrics.description: The optional stopping theorem's inequality E[X_τ] ≤ E[X0] for supermartingales implies that strategies involving stopping times do not turn a negative-expected-value game into a positive-expected-value one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this phrase as intuition: optional stopping cannot be exploited to beat the expectation unless hypotheses fail (e.g., unbounded stopping times with unbounded increments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary of optional stopping (42.5.5): submartingale and martingale cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the same hypotheses as the optional stopping theorem: if (Xn) is a submartingale then E[X_τ] ≥ E[X0]; if it is a martingale then E[X_τ] = E[X0].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply by negating (for submartingale) or noting both inequalities (for martingale). This lets you compute probabilities or expected values when you can express the desired quantity as E[X_τ] of a martingale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Martingale method for computing probabilities (Ballot problem example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model the combinatorial event with a martingale (modify a raw process to enforce the martingale property), choose a stopping time τ that corresponds to the event of interest, then use E[X_τ] = E[X0] to relate known initial expectation to the probability of the event (e.g., making X_τ equal 1 on the desired event and 0 otherwise so that E[X_τ] is the probability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: For the ballot problem define Xi = (Ai − Bi)/(a + b − i) (or equivalent) so Xi is a martingale on 0 ≤ i ≤ a+b−1, take τ to be the time Alice first falls behind (or a+b−1 if she stays ahead), then E[X_τ] = E[X0] yields the desired probability a−b over a+b. This is a pattern: construct martingale with terminal indicator form, apply optional stopping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wald's identity (Problem 42C) — conditions and conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X1, X2, ... be independent random variables with mean μ. Let τ be a stopping time with E[τ] < ∞ and the event {τ = n} depends only on X1,...,Xn. Then E[X1 + ... + X_τ] = μ E[τ].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an expectation identity useful when summing a random number of i.i.d. terms; verify the stopping time dependence condition and finite expectation of τ before applying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total derivative as linear approximation (Definition 43.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f : U ⊆ V → W and p ∈ U, a linear map T : V → W is the total derivative (Df)_p if lim_{∥v∥→0} ∥f(p+v) − f(p) − T(v)∥_W / ∥v∥_V = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret the derivative as the best linear approximation at a point. Use norms on domain and codomain to quantify the approximation. Differentiability implies continuity. Example: for f(x,y)=x^2+y^2, (Df)_p = 2a e∨_1 + 2b e∨_2 at p=(a,b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection principle (Theorem 43.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If W is m-dimensional with basis w1,...,wm, there is a bijection between continuous (or differentiable/smooth) functions f:U→W and m-tuples of scalar functions f1,...,fm:U→R given by projection: f(v)=∑ fi(v) wi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces many multivariable problems with vector-valued codomain to the scalar-valued case by working coordinatewise; used repeatedly to treat Df as collection of partials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial derivatives and relation to total derivative (Definition 43.3.1 and remarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a basis e1,...,en for V, the ith partial derivative ∂f/∂ei at p is lim_{t→0} (f(p+tei)−f(p))/t. If (Df)_p exists then (Df)_p(ei) = ∂f/∂ei(p), and Df = ∑ (∂f/∂ei) e∨_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of Df as a map U→V∨ and of partials as its coordinate functions. Each partial is a scalar function on U. Use this to compute total derivatives by computing partial derivatives in coordinates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous partials imply differentiability (Theorem 43.3.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If all partial derivatives ∂f/∂ei exist on U and are continuous, then f is differentiable and Df = ∑ (∂f/∂ei) e∨_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theorem gives a practical sufficient condition to compute Df using familiar partial derivatives. Beware: continuity of partials is necessary in the theorem — the condition cannot be dropped (counterexample provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher derivatives and symmetry of second derivative (Theorem 43.4.2 & Corollary 43.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If D^2 f exists at p, then D^2 f is symmetric: (D^2 f)_p(v1,v2) = (D^2 f)_p(v2,v1). Consequently (Clairaut) mixed partials commute where second derivatives exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supports treating the Hessian as a symmetric matrix and ensures equality of mixed second partial derivatives under the stated differentiability hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of differential k-form (44.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A differential k-form α on an open set U ⊆ V is a smooth map α : U → Λ^k(V∨) (the k-th exterior power of the dual space).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret a k-form at a point p as a multilinear alternating map that eats k tangent vectors and returns a signed volume; low-degree examples: 0-forms = functions, 1-forms = elements of V∨ (e.g., df).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to evaluate wedge products on vectors (Definition 44.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition yields the alternating multilinear pairing used to interpret k-forms as signed volumes; it enforces antisymmetry properties like ξ∧η = −η∧ξ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exterior derivative for forms and coordinate formula (Definition 44.4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If α = ∑_I f_I d e_I, then dα := ∑_I df_I ∧ d e_I = ∑_{I,j} (∂f_I/∂e_j) d e_j ∧ d e_I. For functions f, df = Df = ∑ (∂f/∂e_i) e∨_i; abuse notation dx_i := d(e∨_i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute d by differentiating coefficient functions and wedging with basis 1-forms. The definition is coordinate-independent though written in coordinates here. Example computations and the notation dx, dy are standard (with admitted abuse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exterior derivative vanishes twice: d^2 = 0 (Theorem 44.4.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any k-form α, applying the exterior derivative twice yields zero: d(dα) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fundamental identity underlies many results (e.g., exact forms are closed). It follows from the antisymmetry of wedge and equality of mixed partial derivatives under regularity hypotheses; practice by computing d^2 on coordinate examples.
